questions.prompt: What is the resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit (ideal L and C)?
questions.explanation:
Resonance occurs when the inductor and capacitor reactances cancel: \(\omega_{0}L=1/(\omega_{0}C)\) ⇒ \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\) (reader Eq. 2.36). It does not depend on R.
• \(\sqrt{LC}\) has wrong units (it is a time).
• \(1/(RC)\) is the corner of an RC filter.
• \(R/L\) is the decay rate scale of an RL circuit, not the resonance of an LC pair.

questions.prompt: What is the series RLC circuit's input impedance Z at resonance \((\omega=\omega_{0})\)?
options: Purely real and equal to R (the minimum magnitude of |Z|)
questions.explanation:
\(Z=R+j\omega L+1/(j\omega C)=R+j(\omega L-1/(\omega C))\). At \(\omega_{0}\) the bracket vanishes: \(Z=R\), which is the smallest |Z| the circuit ever has, so the current is largest (reader Sec. 2.5.3).
• Infinite impedance is the PARALLEL LC resonance.
• The resistor is still in series, so Z cannot be zero.
• The reactances cancel rather than add.

A series RLC circuit has \(R=20\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\) and \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). What is its quality factor \(Q=\omega_{0}L/R\)?

questions.prompt: For the series RLC circuit of the previous problem (\(R=20\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), \(Q=5\)), with the output taken across R, what is the −3 dB bandwidth \(\Delta f\) in hertz? \((\Delta\omega=\omega_{0}/Q.)\)
questions.explanation:
\(\Delta\omega=\omega_{0}/Q=10^{4}/5=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (also \(R/L=20/0.01=2000\checkmark\)).
\(\Delta f=\Delta\omega/(2\pi)=2000/6.2832=318.3\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
Common mistake: stating \(2000\ (\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s})\) as the answer in Hz. (Numerically solving \(|H|^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\) gives \(\omega_{+}-\omega_{-}=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) exactly.)
questions.figure_alt: Band-pass magnitude of the series RLC peaking at 0 dB at omega0 = 10^4 rad/s.

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit has \(Q=5\) and is driven by a source of amplitude 2 V at its resonant frequency. What is the amplitude of the voltage across the inductor?
questions.explanation:
At resonance I \(=V_{s}/R\), so \(V_{L}=j\omega_{0}L\cdot I=j\omega_{0}L\cdot V_{s}/R=jQ\cdot V_{s}\). Amplitude \(=Q\times 2\ \mathrm{V}=10\ \mathrm{V}\), leading the source by 90° (reader Eq. 2.37). The capacitor voltage has the same magnitude and opposite sign, so \(V_{L}+V_{C}=0\) and the source voltage appears entirely across R.
• 2 V forgets the voltage multiplication.
• 0 V confuses the net reactive voltage (which is zero) with the individual element voltage.
• 50 V uses \(Q^{2}\) instead of Q.

questions.prompt: In a series RLC circuit (output across R), the resistance R is doubled while L and C stay the same. Which set of statements is correct?
options: \(\omega_{0}\) is unchanged, Q is halved, the bandwidth doubles, and the peak gain \(|H(j\omega_{0})|\) is still 1
\(\omega_{0}\) doubles, Q is halved, the bandwidth is unchanged, and the peak gain is still 1
\(\omega_{0}\) is unchanged, Q is halved, the bandwidth doubles, and the peak gain is halved
\(\omega_{0}\) falls by \(\sqrt{2}\), Q doubles, the bandwidth halves, and the peak gain is still 1
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\) does not contain R, so it is unchanged. \(Q=\omega_{0}L/R\) halves. The bandwidth \(\Delta\omega=\omega_{0}/Q=R/L\) doubles. At resonance, L and C cancel and \(V_{R}=V_{s}\), so the peak gain is 1 regardless of R (reader: 'the peak gain is always unity, regardless of Q').
Each wrong option makes at least one error: R does not set \(\omega_{0}\), a larger R makes the circuit LESS selective (wider, not narrower), and the peak of \(V_{R}/V_{s}\) does not depend on R.

questions.prompt: A series RLC band-pass circuit (output across R) has \(\omega_{0}=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(Q=1\). What is the exact UPPER −3 dB frequency \(\omega_{+}\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)? (The approximation \(\omega_{0}+\Delta\omega/2\) is not accurate at low Q.)
questions.explanation:
Set \(|H|^{2}=1/2\), i.e., \((\omega_{0}^{2}-\omega^{2})/(\omega_{0}\omega/Q)=\pm 1\). For the upper edge: \(\omega^{2}+(\omega_{0}/Q)\omega-\omega_{0}^{2}=0\), so \(\omega_{+}=\omega_{0}[\sqrt{1+1/(4Q^{2})}+1/(2Q)]\).
With \(Q=1\): \(\omega_{+}=1000(\sqrt{1.25}+0.5)=1000(1.1180+0.5)=1618\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). The lower edge is \(\omega_{-}=1000(1.1180-0.5)=618.0\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
Note \(\omega_{+}-\omega_{-}=1000=\omega_{0}/Q\checkmark\) and \(\sqrt{\omega_{+}\omega_{-}}=1000=\omega_{0}\) (geometric mean). The naive estimate \(\omega_{0}+\Delta\omega/2=1500\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) is 7% too low.
questions.figure_alt: Broad band-pass magnitude centered at 1000 rad/s.

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit has \(Q=0.5\), and the output is the voltage across the capacitor. Which statement about \(|V_{C}/V_{s}|\) versus frequency is correct?
options: It peaks at exactly \(\omega_{0}\) with a peak value of \(Q=0.5\)
It peaks at \(\omega_{0}\) with a peak value of 1
It rises above 1 near \(\omega_{0}\) because the capacitor voltage is multiplied by Q
It starts at 1 at DC and decreases monotonically; there is no resonant peak, and at \(\omega_{0}\) it equals \(Q=0.5\)
questions.explanation:
\(H_{C}=1/(1-(\omega/\omega_{0})^{2}+j(\omega/\omega_{0})/Q)\). For \(Q=0.5\) the poles are real and coincident (critical damping): \(|H_{C}|=1/(1+(\omega/\omega_{0})^{2})\), which falls monotonically from 1. At \(\omega_{0}\) it equals \(Q=0.5\).
The 'voltage multiplication by Q' only produces a peak when Q is large enough (peaking exists only for \(Q>1/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.707\)). For \(Q\approx 10\) the peak is near \(\omega_{0}\) and \(\approx Q\), but here Q < 0.707 so there is none.
• The first wrong option claims a peak of 0.5 (lower than the DC gain of 1).
• A peak of 1 at \(\omega_{0}\) would be the R-output of the circuit, not the C-output.
questions.figure_alt: Capacitor-output magnitude of a Q = 0.5 series RLC versus normalized frequency.

questions.prompt: Preview of stability. A later skill analyzes feedback amplifiers whose closed-loop response has the denominator \(s^{2}+2\times 10^{5}\cdot s+10^{12}\ (s\) in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)). Compare it with the series-RLC form \(s^{2}+(R/L)s+1/(LC)=s^{2}+(\omega_{0}/Q)s+\omega_{0}^{2}\) . What Q does this feedback amplifier have?
questions.explanation:
Match coefficients: \(\omega_{0}^{2}=10^{12}\) ⇒ \(\omega_{0}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). \(\omega_{0}/Q=2\times 10^{5}\) ⇒ \(Q=10^{6}/(2\times 10^{5})=5\).
A Q of 5 means a lightly damped, strongly peaking response: the poles are very close to the \(j\omega\) axis, where an amplifier would ring badly or oscillate. Keeping Q low enough (well below 1) is a key goal of the stability skill. Common mistake: using \(Q=\omega_{0}/(2\times 2\times 10^{5})=2.5\); the s-coefficient is \(\omega_{0}/Q\) itself, with no extra factor of 2.

questions.prompt: Preview of coupling capacitors and frequency response. A real 100 nF capacitor has a parasitic series inductance (ESL) of 10 nH, so it behaves like a series LC. Using the series-resonance formula, at what frequency (in MHz) does it stop acting like a capacitor and start behaving inductively?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}=1/\sqrt{10^{-8}\times 10^{-7}}=1/\sqrt{10^{-15}}=3.162e+07\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
\(f_{0}=\omega_{0}/(2\pi)=5.033\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Above \(f_{0}\) the inductor's reactance exceeds the capacitor's and the part looks like an inductor, so a 'coupling capacitor' is no longer a good signal path (or bypass).
Common mistake: forgetting to divide by \(2\pi\) (giving \(31.6\ \mathrm{Mrad}/\mathrm{s}\approx 31.6'\mathrm{MHz}\)').

questions.prompt: Preview of op-amp frequency response. A closed-loop op-amp stage has a second-order low-pass response \(H=\omega_{0}^{2}/(s^{2}+(\omega_{0}/Q)s+\omega_{0}^{2})\), which at \(s=j\omega_{0}\) has magnitude Q (the same voltage multiplication you saw for the series RLC's capacitor). With \(Q=1.5\), what is the output amplitude for a 0.2 V amplitude tone at \(\omega=\omega_{0}\)?
questions.explanation:
At \(\omega=\omega_{0}\): \(H=\omega_{0}^{2}/(-\omega_{0}^{2}+j(\omega_{0}^{2}/Q)+\omega_{0}^{2})=\omega_{0}^{2}/(j\omega_{0}^{2}/Q)=Q/j\), so \(|H|=Q=1.5\).
Output amplitude \(=0.2\ \mathrm{V}\times 1.5=0.3\ \mathrm{V}\): a 'gain 1' amplifier actually amplifies tones near \(\omega_{0}\) by 50%, i.e., about +3.5 dB of peaking. This is the same phenomenon as an RLC resonance, and it limits the usable bandwidth of the stage.
Common mistake: assuming \(|H|\le 1\) because the DC gain is 1.
questions.figure_alt: Second-order low-pass magnitude with a resonant peak near omega0.
